{{short description|On least area of curves of constant width}}
[[File:Reuleaux supporting lines.svg|thumb|A [[Reuleaux triangle]], a [[curve of constant width]] whose area is minimum among all convex sets with the same width]]
In [[plane geometry]] the '''Blaschke–Lebesgue theorem''' states that the [[Reuleaux triangle]] has the least area of all [[Curve of constant width|curves of given constant width]].{{r|gruber}} In the form that every curve of a given width has area at least as large as the Reuleaux triangle, it is also known as the '''Blaschke–Lebesgue inequality'''.{{r|marmono}} It is named after [[Wilhelm Blaschke]] and [[Henri Lebesgue]], who published it separately in the early 20th century.

==Statement==
The width of a convex set <math>K</math> in the [[Euclidean plane]] is defined as the minimum distance between any two parallel lines that enclose it. The two minimum-distance lines are both necessarily [[tangent line]]s to <math>K</math>, on opposite sides. A [[curve of constant width]] is the boundary of a convex set with the property that, for every direction of parallel lines, the two tangent lines with that direction that are tangent to opposite sides of the curve are at a distance equal to the width. These curves include both the circle and the [[Reuleaux triangle]], a curved triangle formed from arcs of three equal-radius circles each centered at a crossing point of the other two circles. The area enclosed by a Reuleaux triangle with width <math>w</math> is
:<math>\frac{1}{2}(\pi - \sqrt3)w^2 \approx 0.70477w^2.</math>
The Blaschke–Lebesgue theorem states that this is the unique minimum possible area of a curve of constant width, and the Blaschke–Lebesgue inequality states that every convex set of width <math>w</math> has area at least this large, with equality only when the set is bounded by a Reuleaux triangle.{{r|gruber}}

==History==
The Blaschke–Lebesgue theorem was published independently in 1914 by [[Henri Lebesgue]]{{r|lebesgue}} and in 1915 by [[Wilhelm Blaschke]].{{r|blaschke}} Since their work, several other proofs have been published.{{r|fujiwara|mayer|eggleston|ghandehari|harell|malagoli}}

==In other planes==
The same theorem is also true in the [[hyperbolic plane]].{{r|araujo}} For any convex [[Metric space|distance function]] on the plane (a distance defined as the [[Norm (mathematics)|norm]] of the vector difference of points, for any norm), an analogous theorem holds true, according to which the minimum-area curve of constant width is an intersection of three metric disks, each centered on a boundary point of the other two.{{r|ohmann|chakerian}} 

==Application==
The Blaschke–Lebesgue theorem has been used to provide an efficient strategy for generalizations of the game of [[Battleship (game)|Battleship]], in which one player has a ship formed by intersecting the integer grid with a convex set and the other player, after having found one point on this ship, is aiming to determine its location using the fewest possible missed shots. For a ship with <math>n</math> grid points, it is possible to bound the number of missed shots by <math>O(\log\log n)</math>.{{r|cdfg}}

==Related problems==
By the [[isoperimetric inequality]], the curve of constant width in the Euclidean plane with the largest area is a [[circle]].{{r|gruber}} The [[perimeter]] of a curve of constant width <math>w</math> is <math>\pi w</math>, regardless of its shape; this is [[Barbier's theorem]].{{r|barbier}}

It is unknown which surfaces of constant width in three-dimensional space have the minimum volume. Bonnesen and Fenchel conjectured in 1934 that the minimizers are the two Meissner bodies obtained by rounding some of the edges of a [[Reuleaux tetrahedron]],{{r|bonfen}} but this remains unproven. In 2011 Anciaux and Guilfoyle {{r|anguil}} proved that the minimizer consists of pieces of spheres and tubes over curves, which is true for the Meissner bodies, thus supporting the conjecture of Bonnesen and Fenchel.
